== Problem ==

A baseball league consists of two four-team divisions. Each team plays every other team in its division <math>N</math> games. Each team plays every team in the other division <math>M</math> games with <math>N>2M</math> and <math>M>4</math>. Each team plays a <math>76</math> game schedule. How many games does a team play within its own division?

<math>\textbf{(A) } 36 \qquad \textbf{(B) } 48 \qquad \textbf{(C) } 54 \qquad \textbf{(D) } 60 \qquad \textbf{(E) } 72 </math>

==Solution 1==
On one team they play <math>3N</math> games in their division and <math>4M</math> games in the other.  This gives <math>3N+4M=76</math>.

Since <math>M>4</math> we start by trying M=5. This doesn't work because <math>56</math> is not divisible by <math>3</math>.

Next, <math>M=6</math> does not work because <math>52</math> is not divisible by <math>3</math>.

We try <math>M=7</math> does work by giving <math>N=16</math> ,<math>~M=7</math> and thus <math>3\times 16=\boxed{\textbf{(B)}~48}</math> games in their division.

<math>M=10</math> seems to work, until we realize this gives <math>N=12</math>, but <math>N>2M</math> so this will not work.

==Solution 2==
<math>76=3N+4M > 10M</math>, giving <math>M \le 7</math>.
Since <math>M>4</math>, we have <math>M=5,6,7</math>.
Since <math>4M</math> is <math>1</math> <math>\pmod{3}</math>, we must have <math>M</math> equal to <math>1</math> <math>\pmod{3}</math>, so <math>M=7</math>.

This gives <math>3N=48</math>, as desired. The answer is <math>\boxed{\textbf{(B)}~48}</math>.

==Solution 3==
Notice that each team plays <imath>N</imath> games against each of the three other teams in its division. So that's <imath>3N</imath>.

Since each team plays <imath>M</imath> games against each of the four other teams in the other division, that's <imath>4M</imath>.

So <imath>3N+4M=76</imath>, with <imath>M>4, N>2M</imath>. 

Let's start by solving this Diophantine equation. In other words, <imath>N=\frac{76-4M}{3}</imath>. 

So <imath>76-4M\equiv0 \pmod{3}</imath> (remember: <imath>M</imath> must be divisible by 3 for <imath>N</imath> to be an integer!). Therefore, after reducing <imath>76</imath> to <imath>1</imath> and <imath>-4M</imath> to <imath>2M</imath> (we are doing things in <imath>\pmod{3}</imath>), we find that <imath>M\equiv1 \pmod{3}</imath>. 

Since <imath>M>4</imath>, so the minimum possible value of <imath>M</imath> is <imath>7</imath>. However, remember that <imath>N>2M</imath>! To find the greatest possible value of M, we assume that <imath>N=2M</imath> and that is the upper limit of <imath>M</imath> (excluding that value because <imath>N>2M</imath>). Plugging <imath>N=2M</imath> in, <imath>10M=76</imath>. So <imath>M<7.6</imath>. Since you can't have <imath>7.6</imath> games, we know that we can only check <imath>M=7</imath> since we know that since <imath>M>4, M<7.6, M\equiv1 \pmod{3}</imath>. After checking <imath>M=7</imath>, we find that it will work.

So <imath>M=7, N=16</imath>. So each team plays 16 games against each team in its division. Since they are asking for games in it division, which equals <imath>3n = 48</imath>. Select <imath>\boxed{\textbf{(B)}~48}</imath>. (P.S: This might be too complicated).
